result.summary: Medea, at Jason's request, rejuvenates his father Æson with a night ritual, herbs gathered from a dragon-drawn chariot flight, and a magic cauldron. She then tricks the daughters of Pelias into killing their own father, promising to make him young but instead dismembering him in the cauldron.

scenes.title: Jason asks for his father's youth
scenes.summary: After the return home, with thanks offered to the gods, Jason begs Medea to give some of his years to the dying Æson.
scenes.stakes: Æson is near death; Jason fears losing his father.

scenes.title: Medea's midnight invocation
scenes.summary: Medea refuses to take Jason's years but promises a greater gift. Under the full moon she calls on Night, Hecate and the powers of nature, recounting her past magic.
scenes.stakes: Medea's success in the rite depends on the gods' help.

scenes.title: Gathering herbs in Thessaly
scenes.summary: In her dragon-drawn chariot Medea flies over Thessalian mountains and rivers for nine days and nights, collecting herbs.

scenes.title: Æson made young again
scenes.summary: Medea performs rites at two altars, brews a potion in a cauldron, and drains Æson's old blood, replacing it with the juices. He regains the vigor of forty years earlier.
scenes.stakes: Æson's life hangs on the success of the rite.

scenes.title: Medea deceives Pelias's daughters
scenes.summary: Medea feigns a quarrel with Jason and takes refuge with Pelias's daughters. She wins their trust by turning an old ram into a lamb.
scenes.stakes: The daughters risk being tricked into harming their father.

scenes.title: The murder of Pelias
scenes.summary: Medea puts Pelias and his guards to sleep and urges his daughters to stab him. They strike blindly and he protests; Medea cuts his throat and throws him in the cauldron.
scenes.stakes: Pelias is killed; the daughters are made parricides.

alias_notes.explanation: Medea is called this from the river Phasis in Colchis.

notable_quotes.reason: Medea's grand invocation listing her magical powers over nature, echoed by Shakespeare's Prospero.
Ironic line: their devotion makes them commit the crime.

analysis.text: Medea's magic is double-edged: the same art that restores Æson destroys Pelias, showing deception and vengeance disguised as help.
The night rites with altars, blood offerings and Hecate reflect Roman ideas of witchcraft and necromantic ritual.

legacy.text: Medea's invocation (sentences 12-13) was adapted by Shakespeare for Prospero's speech in The Tempest, 'Ye elves of hills, brooks...'.

fun_facts.text: The story of Pelias's death at his daughters' hands was also told in Greek tradition, including a lost play by Euripides, Peliades.

language_notes.text: Hæmonian is a poetic name for Thessaly, Jason's homeland; Hæmonian mothers and fathers are the families of the returned Argonauts.
Medea betrayed her father Æetes and left him behind when she fled with Jason, so Jason's love for his father shames her.
"Goddess of the triple form" is Hecate, worshipped as three-bodied or three-faced, linked with the moon, the underworld and crossroads.
Temesæan brass: people clashed bronze (from Temesa) to relieve the moon during eclipses, which they thought were caused by witches' spells.
The "grandsire" is the Sun, Medea's grandfather; she claims her spells can pale his chariot. Aurora is the dawn goddess.
Refers to Jason's tasks in Colchis: yoking the fire-breathing bulls and ploughing the field with them, thanks to Medea's protective drugs.
Recalls the dragon's-teeth warriors who fought one another, and the sleepless dragon guarding the Golden Fleece, which Medea drugged.
Tempe, Ossa, Pelion, Othrys, Pindus and Olympus are Thessalian valleys and mountains, famed in myth and rich in herbs, which suits Medea's search.
Glaucus was a fisherman who ate a magic herb at Anthedon and became a sea-god. The herb's power was still not widely known.
She avoids contact with her husband Jason because the rite requires ritual purity. She also stays outside the house, under open sky.
The king of the shades is Pluto, and his ravished wife is Proserpina, whom he carried off to the underworld.
Worshippers of Bacchus (Greek Dionysus) were known for ecstatic frenzy, with loose hair and torches in their rites.
Ambiguous wolf means a werewolf, a creature able to change between wolf and man.
Slough is a snake's cast-off skin.
Barbarian here means foreign, since Medea comes from Colchis; it is not a judgment of her character.
Liber is another name for Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus), god of wine. His nurses, the nymphs of Nysa, were earlier rejuvenated by Medea's art.
"Phasian" and "Colchian" both refer to Medea, who came from Colchis, where the river Phasis flows.
"Hæmonian" means Thessalian; Hæmonia was an old name for Thessaly, famed for witchcraft.
Phœbus taking the yoke off his horses three times means three days have passed; the sun god's chariot sets in the western sea.
A paradox: the more dutiful each daughter is, the more undutiful her act. Their affection is what drives them to the crime.

context_notes.text: This summary is the translator's heading. Medea, a Colchian sorceress and Jason's wife, here uses magic to rejuvenate Æson.
Æson is Jason's aged father; Pelias, Jason's uncle, had usurped the throne and sent Jason for the Golden Fleece.
Medea's rite follows ancient magic practice: night-time, loose hair, bare feet, repeated threes, and calls to Hecate, goddess of witchcraft.
Hecate was the goddess of witchcraft, night and crossroads, Medea's patron. Youth (Hebe) is the goddess invoked to restore Æson's vigor.
Black animals and blood poured into trenches were typical offerings to underworld deities.
Purifying three times with fire, water and sulphur was a standard cleansing ritual. Three was a sacred number.
Æson is Jason's aged father. Medea gives back his youth at Jason's request.
Pelias, king of Iolcos, had usurped the throne and sent Jason for the Golden Fleece. Medea now takes revenge on him for Jason.
The daughters are the Peliades. Medea tricks them into killing their own father, and her promise of rejuvenation is false.

literary_notes.text: "What can enchantments not effect?" shows Jason's faith in Medea's power and foreshadows the terrible uses she will make of it.
Medea's concealed feelings and the memory of her abandoned father show a conflicted, secretive character beneath her power.
The repeated "three times" and the long catalogue of powers build a ritual rhythm and show the vast scope of Medea's claimed control.
The sleeping world and still air create an eerie hush that sets off Medea's lone, restless figure and the coming magic.
Medea addresses Night, the Stars, Hecate and the Earth directly, as if they were listening allies.
The dragons feed only on fumes yet shed their old skins. This marvel shows the herbs' power before the main miracle.
The list of strange ingredients builds an atmosphere of eerie, exotic magic through accumulation.
The dry olive branch turning green and fruitful previews Æson's coming rejuvenation as a small test of the potion.
Leanness 'flies, being expelled', as if the signs of age were beings driven out of his body.
The "herbs without any virtue" are powerless, signalling that the promised rejuvenation is a lie and that the daughters are being tricked.
Ovid turns virtue into vice: love for their father makes them guilty of killing him.
Pelias's helpless question to his daughters makes the horror of the murder more affecting.
Cutting off his throat "together with his words" joins a physical act and speech, so his protest is silenced mid-utterance.
